title: Build your own AI project manager
use_case: Create my own AI project manager that scopes a project, then monitors and reports on execution.
outcome: A working assistant that turns a project brief into a structured scope, then reads live project data such as tracker tasks, dates and meeting notes, flags slippage and risks, and drafts a weekly status report for human approval. You also gain the judgement to decide when to buy a tool instead of building one.
assumptions: You are willing to learn or refresh basic Python. Most building steps assume it.
Your projects live in a tracker such as Jira, Asana, monday.com, Microsoft Planner or GitHub Projects, plus shared documents.
A human approves scopes and status reports before they go out, at least during the pilot.

capabilities.name: Frame AI for project management
capabilities.why: Decide which project-management tasks the assistant should do, which it should only draft, and which stay with people, before writing any code.

steps.why: Free, one-hour PMI view of where generative AI helps and where it creates risk in project work.
A practical framework for delegating to AI and checking its output, which is the core of the assistant's design.
PMI's certification in scoping and running AI projects. Useful if you will also lead AI delivery for others; adds a recognised credential.

capabilities.name: Python foundations
capabilities.why: Agent frameworks, tracker APIs and MCP servers are mostly used from Python.

steps.why: Skip if you already write Python. Otherwise take it before capability 3.

capabilities.name: Build with an LLM API: prompts, structured output and tool use
capabilities.why: Scoping means turning a brief into consistent, structured output (objectives, deliverables, work breakdown, risks), and monitoring means calling tools to fetch data.

steps.why: Hands-on API course covering prompt engineering, prompt evaluation and tool use.

capabilities.name: Design agents that plan, act and check their own work
capabilities.why: A project manager agent must break goals into steps, decide which tool to call, and reflect on results before reporting.

steps.why: Agent design patterns (reflection, tool use, planning, multi-agent) from Andrew Ng, with practical exercises.
Deeper, project-based practice with agent frameworks including LangGraph, with an assessed certificate.
Free lessons on agent design patterns, planning and multi-agent systems; useful if you work in Microsoft tooling.

capabilities.name: Connect to project tools and data
capabilities.why: The assistant needs read access, and later limited write access, to your tracker, documents and chat to see real progress.

steps.why: One-hour introduction to the Model Context Protocol, the standard way to plug tools and data into an AI assistant.
Build an MCP server and connect an assistant to it and to existing open-source servers.

capabilities.gap: No verified course yet teaches the specific tracker APIs (Jira, Asana, monday.com, Microsoft Planner) or workflow-automation platforms (for example n8n, Power Automate, Zapier) for this purpose. Use each vendor's API documentation for now.

capabilities.name: Retrieve context from project documents
capabilities.why: Status reports must draw on charters, RAID logs, decisions and meeting notes, not just task dates, so the assistant needs retrieval over documents (RAG).

steps.why: Free, project-based course in building and evaluating RAG systems.
A more structured, longer route through RAG and agentic AI, with a Coursera certificate.

capabilities.name: Evaluate and trust the reports
capabilities.why: A status report that invents progress or misses a slipped milestone is worse than none. You need test cases and measurable accuracy before relying on it.

steps.why: In-depth course on evaluating LLM products, including error analysis. Expensive; take it if the assistant will be used beyond your own projects.

capabilities.gap: Prompt evaluation (capability 3) and RAG evaluation (capability 6) cover the basics. No verified course yet covers monitoring agents in production (tracing and observability tools).

capabilities.name: Govern access, oversight and accountability
capabilities.why: The assistant reads sensitive project and people data and may influence decisions, so it needs clear permissions, human oversight and an audit trail.

steps.why: Short, highly rated overview of AI governance and oversight principles to apply to your own agent.

capabilities.name: Run it on a schedule, unattended
capabilities.why: Monitoring only works if the assistant runs on its own, for example every morning or every Friday, with secrets, logs and failure alerts.
capabilities.gap: No verified course in the database yet teaches scheduling and hosting a small agent (cron jobs, serverless functions, workflow tools, secrets handling). Research candidates are listed below.

milestones.name: Write the assistant's job description
milestones.deliverable: One-page spec: inputs (tracker, documents, meetings), outputs (scope document, weekly status report), what it may decide versus escalate, and how you will judge success.

milestones.name: Scoping assistant
milestones.deliverable: A script that turns a project brief into a structured scope (objectives, deliverables, work breakdown, milestones, risks, assumptions) as JSON plus a readable document, reviewed by you.

milestones.name: Read-only tracker connection
milestones.deliverable: The assistant lists tasks, owners, due dates and status from your tracker through an existing or self-built MCP server, with no write access.

milestones.name: Monitoring and status report
milestones.deliverable: Weekly report comparing plan with actuals, a red/amber/green status per workstream, flagged slippage and risks, and citations to the source tasks and notes.

milestones.name: Evaluation set
milestones.deliverable: 20 or more past weeks with your own correct status as the answer key, plus a scored comparison of the assistant's reports and a log of its errors.

milestones.name: Supervised pilot
milestones.deliverable: Scheduled weekly run with human approval before sending, an access review, an audit log, and a short buy-versus-build note comparing it with your tracker's built-in AI features.

research_queue: Credible training on tracker APIs and automation: Atlassian (Jira, Rovo agents), Asana, monday.com, Microsoft Planner and Power Automate, n8n.
Microsoft Copilot Studio agent training, if your organisation uses Microsoft 365.
LLM observability and agent monitoring courses (tracing, cost and quality dashboards).
Deploying and scheduling small agents (serverless, cron, managed agent platforms) with course-specific evidence.
notes: No single verified course teaches this use case end to end. The pack combines courses and fills the rest with build milestones.
Many tracker vendors now ship built-in AI features. Compare them with your milestone 1 spec before building everything yourself.
Start read-only. Give the assistant write access, such as updating tasks or sending reports, only after the evaluation set shows it is reliable.
